title: Cell Cycle, Mitosis & Meiosis
description: Cell-cycle phases, mitosis stages, chromosome counts, meiosis I vs II, crossing over, nondisjunction, checkpoints, MPF, p53 and oncogenes vs tumor suppressors.

cards.title: In which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA replicated?
cards.body:
**S phase** (synthesis).

Order: G1 → S → G2 → M. G1, S and G2 together make up interphase, often about 90% of the cycle, and the cell grows throughout it.

Key idea: the M phase is mitosis plus cytokinesis.
cards.searchQuery: S phase DNA replication cell cycle

cards.title: A human body cell has finished S phase and is now in G2. How many chromosomes does it contain?
cards.body:
**46**, made up of 92 sister chromatids.

Replication doubles the DNA but not the chromosome number: each chromosome now has two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

Tip: count centromeres to count chromosomes.

Watch out: the count briefly doubles to 92 only in anaphase, when sisters separate.
cards.searchQuery: chromosome number G2 human cell 46 chromosomes 92 chromatids

cards.title: List the five stages of mitosis in order.
cards.body:
**Prophase → prometaphase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase**.

Cytokinesis usually overlaps the end of telophase.

Watch out: some texts fold prometaphase into prophase and list only four stages (PMAT).
cards.searchQuery: mitosis stages order prophase prometaphase metaphase anaphase telophase

cards.title: In which stage of mitosis does the nuclear envelope fragment, letting spindle microtubules reach and attach to the chromosomes?
cards.body:
**Prometaphase**.

Each chromatid now has a kinetochore, and kinetochore microtubules start moving the chromosomes toward the cell's midline.

Key idea: four-stage schemes call this late prophase.
cards.searchQuery: prometaphase nuclear envelope fragments spindle attaches kinetochore

cards.title: What protein structure forms at the centromere of each sister chromatid and is where spindle microtubules attach?
cards.body:
The **kinetochore**.

Don't mix up three similar terms:

- **Centromere**: the DNA region where sister chromatids are most tightly joined.
- **Centrosome**: the microtubule-organizing center at each spindle pole (with a pair of centrioles in animal cells).
- **Kinetochore**: the attachment site for spindle microtubules.
cards.searchQuery: kinetochore centromere spindle microtubule attachment

cards.title: During cytokinesis in a plant cell, what structure forms from fused Golgi-derived vesicles and develops into the new cell wall?
cards.body:
The **cell plate**.

A rigid wall means plant cells can't pinch in two.

Example: animal cells instead form a **cleavage furrow**, in which a contractile ring of actin microfilaments, interacting with myosin, tightens until the cell splits.
cards.searchQuery: cell plate plant cytokinesis Golgi vesicles new cell wall

cards.title: Which meiotic division separates homologous chromosomes, and which separates sister chromatids?
cards.body:
**Meiosis I** separates homologs (the reductional division: diploid → haploid). **Meiosis II** separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis.

Example: in humans, one 2n = 46 cell gives two cells with 23 duplicated chromosomes after meiosis I, then four haploid cells with 23 chromosomes each.
cards.searchQuery: meiosis I versus meiosis II homologs sister chromatids separate

cards.title: When during meiosis does crossing over occur, and between which chromatids?
cards.body:
In **prophase I**, between **nonsister** chromatids of a homologous pair held together in synapsis.

The X-shaped sites where it has happened are chiasmata. It creates recombinant chromosomes that combine maternal and paternal alleles.

Watch out: exchanges between sister chromatids create no new allele combinations, since sisters are identical.
cards.searchQuery: crossing over prophase I nonsister chromatids chiasmata

cards.title: Independent orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I alone allows how many chromosome combinations in human gametes?
cards.body:
$2^{23}$, about 8.4 million (23 pairs, each able to line up 2 ways).

Random fertilization then allows about 70 trillion ($2^{23} \times 2^{23} = 2^{46}$) zygote combinations, before crossing over adds even more variation.

Key idea: for $n$ chromosome pairs, the number of possible gametes is $2^n$.
cards.searchQuery: independent assortment 2^23 combinations human gametes

cards.title: If nondisjunction occurs in meiosis I vs meiosis II, what fraction of the resulting gametes is abnormal in each case?
cards.body:
**Meiosis I**: all four gametes are abnormal (two $n+1$, two $n-1$). **Meiosis II**: half are (one $n+1$, one $n-1$, two normal).

An $n+1$ gamete fused with a normal one gives a trisomic zygote ($2n+1$); an $n-1$ gamete gives a monosomic one ($2n-1$).

Tip: errors earlier in meiosis affect more of the gametes.
cards.searchQuery: nondisjunction meiosis I versus meiosis II abnormal gametes

cards.title: Down syndrome usually results from having three copies of which chromosome?
cards.body:
**Chromosome 21** (trisomy 21), usually from nondisjunction; the risk rises with maternal age.

Sex-chromosome examples: XXY is Klinefelter syndrome (male); XO is Turner syndrome (female), the only viable human monosomy.
cards.searchQuery: Down syndrome trisomy 21 nondisjunction chromosome

cards.title: Which checkpoint is the key 'go/no-go' decision for many cells, after which the cell usually completes the whole cycle?
cards.body:
The **G1 checkpoint** (called the restriction point in mammalian cells).

Without a go-ahead signal such as a growth factor, the cell exits into **G0**, a nondividing state.

Example: most body cells are in G0; mature nerve and muscle cells never divide, but liver cells can be called back into the cycle after injury.
cards.searchQuery: G1 checkpoint restriction point go ahead G0

cards.title: What must be true before the M-phase (spindle) checkpoint lets a cell begin anaphase?
cards.body:
Every chromosome must be attached to spindle microtubules at its kinetochores, with sister kinetochores attached to **opposite poles**, and aligned at the metaphase plate.

Why: any unattached kinetochore delays anaphase, which keeps daughter cells from getting missing or extra chromosomes.
cards.searchQuery: spindle assembly checkpoint metaphase anaphase kinetochore attachment

cards.title: Which cyclin–Cdk complex, once enough accumulates in late G2, triggers the cell's passage past the G2 checkpoint into M phase?
cards.body:
**MPF** (maturation-promoting factor, also called M-phase-promoting factor).

Cdk levels stay fairly constant; **cyclin** builds up during S and G2 and activates Cdk.

Why: during anaphase, MPF switches itself off by triggering the breakdown of its own cyclin.
cards.searchQuery: MPF cyclin Cdk G2 checkpoint maturation promoting factor

cards.title: Which tumor-suppressor protein, nicknamed the 'guardian of the genome', halts the cell cycle when DNA is damaged?
cards.body:
**p53**.

This transcription factor switches on p21 (which binds Cdks and stops the cycle), DNA-repair genes, and, if the damage can't be fixed, genes that trigger apoptosis.

Example: the p53 gene is mutated in roughly half of all human cancers.
cards.searchQuery: p53 tumor suppressor guardian of the genome DNA damage

cards.title: Why is one mutated allele of a proto-oncogene enough to promote cancer, while tumor-suppressor genes usually need both alleles lost?
cards.body:
Proto-oncogene mutations are **gain of function**; tumor-suppressor mutations are **loss of function**.

One hyperactive allele (now an oncogene, e.g., ras) is enough, like a stuck accelerator. With a tumor suppressor, one working allele still makes enough protein, so both copies must be lost (e.g., p53, BRCA1), like failed brakes.

Key idea: cancer usually needs several such mutations.
cards.searchQuery: proto-oncogene oncogene versus tumor suppressor gain loss of function

cards.title: By what process do prokaryotes reproduce?
cards.body:
**Binary fission**.

The circular chromosome is copied from its origin of replication, the two copies move apart, and the cell splits in two by growth of the membrane and cell wall at the middle.

Watch out: there is no spindle and no mitosis in prokaryotes.
cards.searchQuery: binary fission prokaryote cell division

cards.title: Which tubulin-like protein forms a ring at the division site in a dividing bacterial cell?
cards.body:
**FtsZ**.

It assembles into a ring at the midpoint and recruits the proteins that build the new cell wall, pinching the cell in two.

Key idea: FtsZ is a distant relative of tubulin, showing a shared evolutionary origin for cytoskeletal proteins.
cards.searchQuery: FtsZ ring bacterial cell division tubulin homolog

cards.title: How many sets of chromosomes does a diploid ($2n$) cell have?
cards.body:
**Two** sets, one inherited from each parent.

Haploid ($n$) cells have one set.

Example: a human body cell has $2n = 46$ chromosomes (two sets of 23); a human gamete has $n = 23$.
cards.searchQuery: diploid cell two sets of chromosomes 2n

cards.title: How many chromosomes are in a normal human egg or sperm cell? Give the number only.
cards.body:
**23**.

That is one of each type: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome (X in an egg; X or Y in a sperm).

Key idea: fertilization restores the diploid number: $23 + 23 = 46$.
cards.searchQuery: human gamete chromosome number 23 haploid

cards.title: What term describes the two chromosomes of a pair, one from each parent, that carry the same genes in the same order?
cards.body:
**Homologous chromosomes** (homologs).

They are the same length with the centromere in the same place, but they may carry different alleles of a given gene.

Watch out: homologs are not identical copies of each other; sister chromatids are.
cards.searchQuery: homologous chromosomes pair same genes different alleles

cards.title: What are the two identical DNA copies of a replicated chromosome, joined along their length and at the centromere, called?
cards.body:
**Sister chromatids**.

They are produced by DNA replication in S phase and held together by proteins called cohesins.

Key idea: once the sisters separate in anaphase, each is called a chromosome again.
cards.searchQuery: sister chromatids identical copies replicated chromosome centromere

cards.title: Which protease cuts cohesin to let sister chromatids separate at the start of anaphase?
cards.body:
**Separase**.

Until then, an inhibitor called securin holds separase inactive. When the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) tags securin for destruction, separase is freed and cuts cohesin.

Why: this makes the separation of all sister pairs sudden and simultaneous.
cards.searchQuery: separase cohesin cleavage anaphase sister chromatid separation

cards.title: Which ubiquitin ligase triggers anaphase by marking securin, and later the cyclins, for destruction?
cards.body:
The **anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C)**.

It becomes active once the spindle checkpoint is satisfied. Destroying securin starts anaphase; destroying mitotic cyclin lets the cell exit mitosis.

Tip: the name tells you its job: it promotes anaphase.
cards.searchQuery: anaphase promoting complex APC/C securin cyclin degradation

cards.title: Around which family of proteins is eukaryotic DNA wrapped to form nucleosomes?
cards.body:
**Histones**.

Eight histone proteins make up a core, and DNA winds around it about twice, like beads on a string. Histones are rich in positively charged amino acids that bind the negatively charged DNA backbone.

Key idea: nucleosomes are the first level of DNA packing; further coiling and looping make a mitotic chromosome.
cards.searchQuery: histones nucleosome DNA packaging chromatin

cards.title: Which protein complexes compact chromosomes into their short, thick mitotic form?
cards.body:
**Condensins**.

They use ATP to loop and coil the chromatin, so the long DNA molecules can be pulled apart without tangling.

Watch out: cohesins hold sister chromatids together; condensins compact each chromatid. Don't confuse the two.
cards.searchQuery: condensin complexes chromosome condensation mitosis

cards.title: What is the name for an organized display of a cell's chromosomes, paired and arranged by size and shape?
cards.body:
A **karyotype**.

Chromosomes are photographed in metaphase, when they are most condensed, then paired by size, banding pattern and centromere position.

Example: a karyotype can reveal an extra chromosome 21 or a missing X.
cards.searchQuery: karyotype chromosomes arranged by size shape metaphase

cards.title: How many pairs of autosomes does a human body cell have? Give the number only.
cards.body:
**22** pairs.

Autosomes are all chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes. The 23rd pair is XX in females and XY in males.

Check: $22 \times 2 + 2 = 46$.
cards.searchQuery: human autosomes 22 pairs sex chromosomes

cards.title: What term describes all body cells except the gametes and their precursors?
cards.body:
**Somatic cells**.

They are diploid and divide by mitosis. Germ-line cells undergo meiosis to make gametes.

Example: skin and liver cells are somatic; the cells in the testis that become sperm are germ-line.
cards.searchQuery: somatic cells versus germ cells diploid mitosis

cards.title: What does mitosis produce, and what is it used for in a multicellular organism?
cards.body:
Two **genetically identical** diploid daughter cells.

Uses: growth, replacement of worn-out cells, and tissue repair. In many single-celled eukaryotes it is the basis of asexual reproduction.

Key idea: mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same, unlike meiosis.
cards.searchQuery: mitosis purpose identical daughter cells growth repair

cards.title: Which phase of the cell cycle varies the most in length among different cell types?
cards.body:
**G1**.

Fast-cycling cells may spend only hours there, while others stay for days or years, or leave the cycle into G0.

Why: S, G2 and M last about the same in most cells of a given species.
cards.searchQuery: G1 phase length varies cell cycle

cards.title: What is the main job of G2 in the cell cycle?
cards.body:
G2 is the second gap phase: the cell continues to grow and **prepares for mitosis**.

It makes proteins needed for mitosis, such as tubulin for the spindle, and the G2 checkpoint confirms that DNA has been fully replicated and is undamaged.

Key idea: it follows DNA replication and precedes M phase.
cards.searchQuery: G2 phase preparation for mitosis G2 checkpoint replication complete

cards.title: A cell in G1 has 2 units of DNA ($2C$). How many units does it have in G2? Give the number only.
cards.body:
**4** ($4C$).

DNA content rises during S phase and stays doubled through G2 and until anaphase ends. It falls back to $2C$ per cell when the cell divides.

Watch out: chromosome number doesn't double in S phase, only DNA content does.
cards.searchQuery: DNA content G1 G2 doubling S phase 2C 4C

cards.title: What are the main events of prophase in animal cell mitosis?
cards.body:
Chromatin **condenses** into visible chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids. The nucleoli disappear, and the **mitotic spindle** begins to assemble as the centrosomes move to opposite poles.

Why: condensing the DNA shortens the chromosomes so they can be separated without breaking.

Watch out: the nuclear envelope is still intact in prophase; it breaks down in prometaphase.
cards.searchQuery: prophase events chromatin condenses spindle begins nucleoli disappear

cards.title: What is the imaginary plane called, midway between the spindle poles, where chromosomes line up in metaphase?
cards.body:
The **metaphase plate**.

Metaphase is the longest stage of mitosis. Each chromosome's kinetochores face opposite poles, held in tension by the spindle.

Watch out: the plate is not a physical structure. Don't confuse it with the cell plate of plant cytokinesis.
cards.searchQuery: metaphase plate chromosomes align midway spindle poles

cards.title: What happens in anaphase of mitosis, and which two movements move the chromosomes apart?
cards.body:
The sister chromatids separate, and each is now a full **chromosome** moving to opposite poles.

- Kinetochore microtubules shorten, pulling chromosomes toward the poles.
- Nonkinetochore microtubules lengthen, pushing the poles apart, and the cell elongates.

Tip: anaphase is the shortest stage of mitosis.
cards.searchQuery: anaphase events sister chromatids separate kinetochore microtubules shorten

cards.title: How many chromosomes does a human cell contain in the middle of anaphase of mitosis? Give the number only.
cards.body:
**92**.

Once the sisters separate, each former chromatid is its own chromosome, so the count doubles from 46 to 92 until the cell divides.

Check: each daughter cell will get 46.
cards.searchQuery: human cell chromosome number anaphase 92 mitosis

cards.title: What are the main events of telophase in mitosis?
cards.body:
Nuclear envelopes **re-form** around each set of chromosomes, the chromosomes **decondense**, nucleoli reappear and the spindle disassembles.

Key idea: telophase more or less reverses prophase and prometaphase.

Example: cytokinesis typically begins during late anaphase or telophase, and separates the two nuclei into two cells.
cards.searchQuery: telophase events nuclear envelope re-forms chromosomes decondense

cards.title: Which spindle microtubules overlap at the cell's midline and lengthen to push the poles apart in anaphase?
cards.body:
**Nonkinetochore microtubules** (also called polar or interpolar microtubules).

Motor proteins slide the overlapping microtubules past each other, elongating the cell.

Key idea: kinetochore microtubules pull; nonkinetochore microtubules push.
cards.searchQuery: nonkinetochore polar microtubules spindle poles apart anaphase

cards.title: What is the radial array of short microtubules extending from each centrosome toward the plasma membrane called?
cards.body:
The **aster**.

Asters help position the spindle in the cell and, in animal cells, help determine where the cleavage furrow forms.

Key idea: the spindle is made of centrosomes, spindle microtubules and asters.
cards.searchQuery: aster microtubules centrosome spindle animal cell mitosis

cards.title: What indentation forms at the cell surface during animal cell cytokinesis?
cards.body:
The **cleavage furrow**.

A contractile ring of actin and myosin pinches the cell in two, like tightening a drawstring.

Key idea: in plants, the new wall instead grows outward from the center as a cell plate.
cards.searchQuery: cleavage furrow animal cell cytokinesis actin myosin ring

cards.title: What results if a cell completes mitosis but cytokinesis fails?
cards.body:
A **binucleate** cell: one cell with two nuclei.

Repeating this gives multinucleate cells.

Example: some tissues, like skeletal muscle fibers, are naturally multinucleate. In others, failed cytokinesis can contribute to cancer by doubling the chromosome number.
cards.searchQuery: failed cytokinesis binucleate cell two nuclei mitosis

cards.title: What is the term for normal cells in culture ceasing to divide when they crowd one another and form a single layer?
cards.body:
**Density-dependent inhibition**.

Crowded cells run low on growth factors and nutrients, and cell-surface proteins sense contact with neighbors and block cell cycle progression.

Why: cancer cells typically ignore this signal and pile up in layers.
cards.searchQuery: density-dependent inhibition cell culture monolayer cancer cells

cards.title: What is the requirement that normal animal cells attach to a surface, such as the extracellular matrix, before they divide?
cards.body:
**Anchorage dependence**.

Signals from integrins and the cytoskeleton at cell attachments tell the cell it may divide.

Example: cancer cells often lack this requirement, so they can grow in suspension and spread to new sites.
cards.searchQuery: anchorage dependence normal cells attach substratum before dividing

cards.title: What are the external protein signals, such as PDGF, that stimulate target cells to divide?
cards.body:
**Growth factors**.

They bind receptors on the cell surface and trigger signaling cascades that push the cell past the G1 checkpoint.

Example: platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), released at wounds, makes fibroblasts divide to heal the injury.
cards.searchQuery: growth factors PDGF stimulate cell division G1 checkpoint

cards.title: What is the ploidy of gametes, written with the letter $n$?
cards.body:
**Haploid** ($n$).

Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so that fusion of two gametes restores the diploid number in the zygote.

Key idea: without meiosis, the chromosome number would double every generation.
cards.searchQuery: gametes haploid n meiosis halves chromosome number

cards.title: How many cells does one complete meiosis produce, and how do they compare genetically?
cards.body:
**Four** haploid cells, each **genetically different**.

Two divisions follow a single round of DNA replication. Crossing over and independent assortment make the products differ from each other and from the parent.

Watch out: mitosis gives two identical diploid cells; meiosis gives four unique haploid cells.
cards.searchQuery: meiosis products four haploid genetically different cells

cards.title: What is the term for the close pairing of homologous chromosomes along their lengths in prophase I?
cards.body:
**Synapsis**.

Homologs align gene by gene, which is what lets crossing over occur between nonsister chromatids.

Key idea: synapsis does not happen in mitosis, where homologs do not pair.
cards.searchQuery: synapsis homologous chromosomes pairing prophase I meiosis

cards.title: Which protein structure zippers homologous chromosomes together during prophase I?
cards.body:
The **synaptonemal complex**.

It forms between the homologs during zygotene and holds them in close alignment while crossing over takes place.

Key idea: it disassembles later in prophase I, leaving the homologs held together only at chiasmata.
cards.searchQuery: synaptonemal complex homologous chromosomes prophase I

cards.title: What name is given to a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes, which contains four chromatids?
cards.body:
A **tetrad** (also called a bivalent).

Two homologs, each made of two sister chromatids, make four chromatids in all.

Example: a human cell in metaphase I has 23 tetrads, not 46 separate chromosomes.
cards.searchQuery: tetrad bivalent four chromatids homologous pair meiosis

cards.title: What is the name for the X-shaped site where homologous chromosomes remain linked after crossing over?
cards.body:
A **chiasma** (plural: chiasmata).

Each marks a place where nonsister chromatids exchanged segments. Chiasmata hold the homologs together until anaphase I.

Why: this linkage helps the pair attach properly to the spindle and separate correctly.
cards.searchQuery: chiasma chiasmata crossing over homologous chromosomes

cards.title: In which substage of prophase I does crossing over take place?
cards.body:
**Pachytene**.

The synaptonemal complex is complete, and the fully paired homologs exchange DNA segments between nonsister chromatids.

Mnemonic: the substages are leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis: "Lazy Zebras Play Dodgeball Daily".
cards.searchQuery: pachytene prophase I crossing over substage

cards.title: List the substages of meiotic prophase I in order.
cards.body:
**Leptotene → zygotene → pachytene → diplotene → diakinesis**.

- Leptotene: chromosomes condense.
- Zygotene: synapsis begins.
- Pachytene: crossing over.
- Diplotene: homologs begin to separate; chiasmata become visible.
- Diakinesis: maximum condensation; the nuclear envelope breaks down.

Tip: prophase I is by far the longest phase of meiosis.
cards.searchQuery: prophase I substages leptotene zygotene pachytene diplotene diakinesis

cards.title: How are chromosomes arranged at metaphase I, and how does this differ from metaphase of mitosis?
cards.body:
**Homologous pairs** (tetrads) line up at the plate, with each homolog facing one pole.

In mitotic metaphase, individual duplicated chromosomes line up single file, with each chromatid facing opposite poles.

Why: this arrangement is what makes the separation of homologs, rather than sisters, possible in anaphase I.
cards.searchQuery: metaphase I homologous pairs align plate versus mitosis metaphase

cards.title: What separates in anaphase I of meiosis, and what stays together?
cards.body:
**Homologous chromosomes** separate. **Sister chromatids** stay attached at their centromeres.

Each chromosome moving to a pole still consists of two chromatids.

Watch out: sisters separate only in anaphase II.
cards.searchQuery: anaphase I homologs separate sister chromatids stay together

cards.title: Is DNA replicated between meiosis I and meiosis II?
cards.body:
**No**.

Meiosis I ends with haploid cells, whose chromosomes still have two chromatids each. Meiosis II separates those chromatids without another S phase.

Why: this is how one round of replication yields four haploid cells with half the DNA of a G1 cell.
cards.searchQuery: DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II no S phase

cards.title: In human oogenesis, what are the small, nonfunctional cells produced by unequal cytokinesis called?
cards.body:
**Polar bodies**.

Each meiosis of a female germ cell gives one large egg plus polar bodies, so nearly all the cytoplasm goes to one cell.

Why: the egg needs stored nutrients and organelles to support early development. Spermatogenesis, by contrast, gives four equal sperm.
cards.searchQuery: polar bodies oogenesis unequal cytokinesis egg

cards.title: In humans, at which stage is a secondary oocyte arrested after ovulation until a sperm penetrates it?
cards.body:
**Metaphase II**.

Fertilization triggers completion of meiosis II, producing the mature egg and a second polar body.

Key idea: an egg is not truly "mature" until it is fertilized.
cards.searchQuery: secondary oocyte arrested metaphase II fertilization completes meiosis

cards.title: Human primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth and then arrest. At which stage do they wait until puberty?
cards.body:
**Prophase I**.

They stay paused there, often for decades, until hormones trigger a few to continue with each cycle.

Why: this long arrest is a reason that the risk of nondisjunction increases with maternal age.
cards.searchQuery: primary oocyte arrested prophase I until puberty

cards.title: Which events occur in meiosis I but not in mitosis?
cards.body:
- **Synapsis** of homologs to form tetrads
- **Crossing over** between nonsister chromatids
- Alignment of homologous **pairs** at metaphase I
- Separation of homologs with sisters kept together

Key idea: these differences explain why meiosis reduces the chromosome number and shuffles alleles.
cards.searchQuery: events unique to meiosis I synapsis crossing over homologs pairs

cards.title: Name the three sources of genetic variation that arise from sexual reproduction.
cards.body:
**Independent assortment** of homologs, **crossing over**, and **random fertilization**.

The first two happen in meiosis, and the third combines gametes at random.

Key idea: mutation is the original source of new alleles; these three processes only reshuffle alleles that already exist.
cards.searchQuery: sources of genetic variation independent assortment crossing over random fertilization

cards.title: What name is given to a chromosome that carries a mix of maternal and paternal alleles because of crossing over?
cards.body:
A **recombinant chromosome**.

Crossing over between nonsister chromatids produces them, so each chromatid may carry a new combination of alleles.

Example: after crossing over, two of the four chromatids in a tetrad are recombinant and two are parental.
cards.searchQuery: recombinant chromosome crossing over maternal paternal alleles

cards.title: An organism has $2n = 6$ (three pairs of chromosomes). How many different gamete types can independent assortment alone produce? Give the number only.
cards.body:
**8**.

The number of combinations is $2^n$, where $n$ is the number of chromosome pairs: $2^3 = 8$.

Watch out: crossing over would make even more types, so this is a minimum.
cards.searchQuery: independent assortment 2n=6 gamete combinations 2^3

cards.title: The fruit fly $\textit{Drosophila}$ has $2n = 8$. How many chromosome combinations can independent assortment produce in its gametes? Give the number only.
cards.body:
**16**.

There are 4 pairs, so the number of combinations is $2^4 = 16$.

Check: human $n = 23$ gives $2^{23} \approx 8.4$ million.
cards.searchQuery: Drosophila 2n=8 gamete combinations independent assortment 2^4

cards.title: In plants and algae with alternation of generations, meiosis in the sporophyte produces which cells?
cards.body:
**Spores**.

Spores are haploid and grow by mitosis into a multicellular gametophyte, which makes gametes by mitosis.

Watch out: in plants, meiosis does not make gametes directly, unlike in animals.
cards.searchQuery: plant alternation of generations meiosis produces spores sporophyte

cards.title: In animals, meiosis directly produces which type of cells?
cards.body:
**Gametes** (sperm and eggs).

They are the only haploid cells in the life cycle, and they fuse at fertilization to form a diploid zygote, which grows by mitosis.

Key idea: animals are diploid for nearly all of their life cycle.
cards.searchQuery: animal life cycle meiosis produces gametes sperm egg

cards.title: In the life cycle of many fungi and some algae, which cell is the only diploid stage?
cards.body:
The **zygote**.

It undergoes meiosis right after fertilization, producing haploid cells that grow by mitosis.

Key idea: in these organisms the haploid stage is dominant, the reverse of animals.
cards.searchQuery: fungi life cycle zygote only diploid cell zygotic meiosis

cards.title: What is the term for the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate properly during meiosis?
cards.body:
**Nondisjunction**.

The result is gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.

Example: if such a gamete is fertilized, the zygote is trisomic ($2n+1$) or monosomic ($2n-1$), which are forms of aneuploidy.
cards.searchQuery: nondisjunction definition failure chromosomes separate meiosis

cards.title: What is the term for a cell with an abnormal number of chromosomes because one or a few are extra or missing?
cards.body:
**Aneuploidy**.

Trisomy ($2n+1$) and monosomy ($2n-1$) are the two main types.

Watch out: this differs from polyploidy, which is having extra whole sets of chromosomes.
cards.searchQuery: aneuploidy abnormal chromosome number trisomy monosomy

cards.title: A female with a single X chromosome and no second sex chromosome (45,X) has which syndrome?
cards.body:
**Turner syndrome**.

Affected females are usually short, with underdeveloped ovaries and typically infertile, but they have normal intelligence in most cases.

Key idea: it is a monosomy, caused by nondisjunction or loss of a sex chromosome.
cards.searchQuery: Turner syndrome 45 X monosomy single X chromosome female

cards.title: A male with an extra X chromosome (47,XXY) has which syndrome?
cards.body:
**Klinefelter syndrome**.

Affected males are usually sterile and may have reduced testosterone and some breast development.

Key idea: the Y chromosome determines male development, so XXY individuals are male despite two X chromosomes.
cards.searchQuery: Klinefelter syndrome 47 XXY extra X chromosome male

cards.title: Trisomy 18, with severe developmental problems and most affected infants not surviving beyond the first year, is named what?
cards.body:
**Edwards syndrome**.

Trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) are the other autosomal trisomies that sometimes survive to birth, though usually only briefly.

Why: most other autosomal trisomies are lethal early in development; chromosome 21 is small and carries relatively few genes.
cards.searchQuery: Edwards syndrome trisomy 18 chromosome

cards.title: Which syndrome results from trisomy 13?
cards.body:
**Patau syndrome**.

It causes severe intellectual disability and physical abnormalities, and most affected infants die within the first year.

Tip: Down is 21, Edwards is 18, Patau is 13: the numbers get smaller as the severity gets worse.
cards.searchQuery: Patau syndrome trisomy 13 chromosome

cards.title: Why does the risk of nondisjunction in the egg rise with a mother's age?
cards.body:
Her primary oocytes have been **arrested in prophase I** since before birth, for decades.

During this long wait, the proteins holding homologs together (cohesins) are thought to deteriorate. Errors in segregation become more likely when meiosis finally resumes.

Key idea: sperm are made continuously from puberty, so they don't wait this long.
cards.searchQuery: maternal age nondisjunction oocytes arrested prophase I cohesin

cards.title: What name is given to the proteins whose concentrations rise and fall through the cell cycle and which activate Cdks?
cards.body:
**Cyclins**.

Their levels oscillate: they are made, accumulate, and are degraded at specific points of the cycle. Cyclin binding turns on its partner Cdk.

Key idea: the rise and fall of cyclin gives the cycle its rhythm.
cards.searchQuery: cyclins concentration fluctuates activate Cdk cell cycle

cards.title: What does the abbreviation Cdk stand for, and what does a Cdk need in order to be active?
cards.body:
**Cyclin-dependent kinase**: a protein kinase that is active only when bound to a **cyclin**.

Active Cdks phosphorylate target proteins, which drives the cell through checkpoints.

Watch out: Cdk concentration stays roughly constant; it is the cyclin level that changes.
cards.searchQuery: Cdk cyclin-dependent kinase active only when bound to cyclin

cards.title: What conditions does the G2 checkpoint verify before the cell enters mitosis?
cards.body:
That the **DNA has been completely replicated** and is **undamaged**.

If not, cyclin–Cdk activity (MPF) is kept off and the cell is held in G2 while repairs are made.

Why: starting mitosis with incomplete or damaged DNA would give daughter cells missing or broken chromosomes.
cards.searchQuery: G2 checkpoint DNA replicated undamaged before mitosis

cards.title: Which Cdk inhibitor protein, switched on by p53, binds cyclin–Cdk complexes and stops the cell cycle?
cards.body:
**p21**.

When DNA is damaged, p53 activates the p21 gene. The p21 protein blocks Cdk activity, so the cell stalls at a checkpoint.

Example: this pause gives the cell time to repair its DNA before copying it.
cards.searchQuery: p21 Cdk inhibitor p53 cell cycle arrest

cards.title: Which tumor suppressor, when unphosphorylated, binds the transcription factor E2F and blocks passage from G1 to S?
cards.body:
**Rb** (retinoblastoma protein).

Cdk phosphorylation of Rb releases E2F, which then turns on genes needed for DNA replication.

Key idea: Rb works as a brake on the G1/S transition that cyclin–Cdk releases.
cards.searchQuery: Rb retinoblastoma protein E2F G1 S transition tumor suppressor

cards.title: What is the term for programmed cell death, in which a cell orderly dismantles itself?
cards.body:
**Apoptosis**.

The cell shrinks, its DNA is cut up, and the remains are packaged in membrane-bound pieces and cleared by neighbors or phagocytes.

Why: this prevents inflammation, unlike necrosis, in which a damaged cell swells and bursts.
cards.searchQuery: apoptosis programmed cell death definition

cards.title: Which family of protein-cutting enzymes carries out apoptosis?
cards.body:
**Caspases**.

They are made as inactive precursors and activate each other in a cascade, cleaving key cell proteins.

Example: DNA damage that p53 can't repair, or signals from other cells, can trigger the cascade.
cards.searchQuery: caspases proteases apoptosis cascade

cards.title: Give two roles of apoptosis in a healthy organism.
cards.body:
- **Shaping development**: e.g., removing the webbing between developing human fingers and toes, or a tadpole's tail.
- **Removing damaged or dangerous cells**: e.g., cells with irreparable DNA damage, or self-reactive immune cells.

Key idea: too little apoptosis can allow cancer to develop; too much can cause tissue loss.
cards.searchQuery: apoptosis roles development webbing fingers remove damaged cells

cards.title: How does apoptosis differ from necrosis?
cards.body:
**Apoptosis** is a controlled, energy-requiring process in which the cell shrinks and is neatly cleared, with little inflammation.

**Necrosis** is uncontrolled death from injury: the cell swells, bursts, and spills its contents, causing **inflammation**.

Tip: apoptosis is cell suicide; necrosis is cell murder.
cards.searchQuery: apoptosis versus necrosis difference inflammation

cards.title: Which small GTP-binding protein, which relays growth factor signals toward the nucleus, is the best-known proto-oncogene?
cards.body:
**Ras**.

Mutations that lock Ras in its active, GTP-bound state send a constant "divide" signal, even without growth factor.

Key idea: Ras is a proto-oncogene; its hyperactive mutant forms are oncogenes. A single mutated allele can be enough.
cards.searchQuery: Ras proto-oncogene GTP-binding protein growth signal cancer

cards.title: Inherited mutations in which tumor-suppressor genes greatly raise the risk of breast and ovarian cancer?
cards.body:
**BRCA1** and **BRCA2**.

Their proteins help repair double-strand breaks in DNA. A person who inherits one mutant copy is at high risk because the other copy is likely to be lost in some cell.

Example: they illustrate why tumor-suppressor mutations are often recessive at the cell level, yet dominant in how the risk is inherited.
cards.searchQuery: BRCA1 BRCA2 tumor suppressor breast ovarian cancer DNA repair

cards.title: How does human papillomavirus (HPV) promote cervical cancer, in terms of tumor suppressors?
cards.body:
Its viral proteins **E6** and **E7** disable p53 and Rb respectively.

E6 targets p53 for destruction, and E7 binds Rb. Without these brakes, infected cells divide unchecked and accumulate mutations.

Key idea: viruses can cause cancer by inactivating tumor suppressors.
cards.searchQuery: HPV E6 E7 inactivate p53 Rb cervical cancer

cards.title: How does a benign tumor differ from a malignant tumor?
cards.body:
A **benign** tumor remains at its original site and is usually not life-threatening.

A **malignant** tumor invades surrounding tissue and can spread to distant sites. Only malignant tumors are called cancer.

Example: a mole is typically benign, but melanoma, a malignant skin tumor, can spread.
cards.searchQuery: benign tumor versus malignant tumor cancer definition

cards.title: What is the term for the spread of cancer cells from the original tumor to distant parts of the body?
cards.body:
**Metastasis**.

Cells invade neighboring tissue, enter blood or lymph vessels, and settle and grow at new sites.

Why: metastasis is the main cause of cancer deaths, since a localized tumor can often be removed.
cards.searchQuery: metastasis cancer spread distant sites blood lymph

cards.title: What is the growth of new blood vessels, which solid tumors stimulate to get oxygen and nutrients, called?
cards.body:
**Angiogenesis**.

Tumors beyond a tiny size release factors such as VEGF that make nearby blood vessels sprout toward them.

Example: some cancer drugs work by blocking these signals so the tumor is starved.
cards.searchQuery: angiogenesis tumor blood vessel growth VEGF

cards.title: What is the limit of roughly 50 divisions that normal human cells can undergo in culture before they stop dividing called?
cards.body:
The **Hayflick limit**.

Telomeres shorten with each division, and critically short telomeres trigger senescence.

Why: most cancer cells reactivate telomerase, which rebuilds telomeres, letting them divide indefinitely.
cards.searchQuery: Hayflick limit cell divisions telomeres senescence cancer telomerase

cards.title: Which abnormal chromosome, created by a 9;22 translocation, carries the $\textit{BCR-ABL}$ fusion gene found in chronic myeloid leukemia?
cards.body:
The **Philadelphia chromosome**.

Pieces of chromosomes 9 and 22 swap, placing the ABL gene next to BCR. The fusion protein is a kinase that is always on.

Example: the drug imatinib (Gleevec) blocks this kinase and treats the disease.
cards.searchQuery: Philadelphia chromosome BCR-ABL translocation 9 22 chronic myeloid leukemia

cards.title: Name three ways a proto-oncogene can be converted into an oncogene.
cards.body:
- **Point mutation** that makes the protein hyperactive (e.g., $\textit{ras}$)
- **Gene amplification**: extra copies make too much protein
- **Chromosomal translocation** that moves the gene next to a strong promoter or fuses it with another gene (e.g., BCR-ABL)

Key idea: each way raises the amount or activity of a growth-promoting protein.
cards.searchQuery: oncogene activation point mutation amplification translocation proto-oncogene

cards.title: What does Knudson's two-hit hypothesis explain about inherited cancers such as hereditary retinoblastoma?
cards.body:
Both copies of a **tumor suppressor** gene must be lost for a tumor to form.

A person who inherits one defective copy (first hit) needs only one more mutation (second hit) in a cell, so tumors form early and often.

Key idea: someone with two normal copies needs two independent mutations in the same cell, which is much less likely.
cards.searchQuery: Knudson two-hit hypothesis retinoblastoma tumor suppressor inherited

cards.title: How does the cancer drug paclitaxel (Taxol) block cell division?
cards.body:
It **stabilizes microtubules**, so spindle microtubules can't depolymerize.

The spindle becomes frozen and rigid, the spindle checkpoint stays on, and the cell is stuck in mitosis and often undergoes apoptosis.

Watch out: other drugs, like vinblastine, do the opposite and prevent spindle assembly; both stop mitosis.
cards.searchQuery: paclitaxel Taxol stabilizes microtubules blocks mitosis cancer drug

cards.title: Which drug is used to arrest dividing cells in metaphase for karyotyping by blocking spindle formation?
cards.body:
**Colchicine**.

It prevents tubulin from polymerizing, so no spindle forms and chromosomes can't be separated. Cells pile up in metaphase, where their chromosomes are most condensed and easiest to count.

Key idea: it is a microtubule poison, so it can also halt other microtubule-based functions.
cards.searchQuery: colchicine metaphase arrest karyotyping spindle inhibitor

cards.title: List four ways cancer cells differ from normal cells in their growth behavior.
cards.body:
- They ignore **checkpoints** and growth-limiting signals
- They lack **density-dependent inhibition** and anchorage dependence
- They can divide indefinitely, often by keeping telomerase active
- They can invade tissues and **metastasize**

Key idea: cancer arises from the accumulation of several mutations, not from one.
cards.searchQuery: cancer cells differ from normal cells checkpoints density inhibition immortal metastasis

cards.title: What name is given to the nondividing state that a cell enters when it leaves the cell cycle in G1?
cards.body:
**G0**.

A cell in G0 is alive and functional but not preparing to divide. Some cells re-enter the cycle when stimulated, and some never do.

Example: mature neurons stay in G0 permanently, while resting liver cells re-enter the cycle after injury.
cards.searchQuery: G0 phase nondividing state exit cell cycle quiescent

cards.title: What is the difference between mitosis and cytokinesis?
cards.body:
**Mitosis** is the division of the nucleus, which separates duplicated chromosomes into two nuclei.

**Cytokinesis** is the division of the cytoplasm, which splits the cell into two daughter cells.

Key idea: they usually go together but are separate processes, as shown by multinucleate cells, where mitosis happened without cytokinesis.
cards.searchQuery: mitosis versus cytokinesis nucleus division cytoplasm division

cards.title: What other name is used for the spindle checkpoint, which delays anaphase until all kinetochores are attached?
cards.body:
The **spindle assembly checkpoint**, or M checkpoint.

Unattached kinetochores send a "wait" signal that keeps the anaphase-promoting complex inactive.

Why: this prevents the premature separation of chromatids and the resulting nondisjunction in mitosis.
cards.searchQuery: spindle assembly checkpoint M checkpoint unattached kinetochores APC

cards.title: What is the cell cycle control system's main internal timing mechanism?
cards.body:
Oscillating **cyclin–Cdk** activity.

Cyclin levels rise and fall, so Cdk is turned on and off at defined points. External signals and checkpoints can pause the clock.

Key idea: a cell cycle checkpoint is a control point where the cycle stops unless a signal gives permission to proceed.
cards.searchQuery: cell cycle control system cyclin Cdk oscillation checkpoint clock
